amendments.rule: **Hebrew has no verb *to have*, so an English *have* is a recasting and belongs to whatever made the clause possessive.** Where `הָיָה` is present it is the existential and takes the *have* itself, its preposition goes `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun: `וַיְהִי לוֹ נָשִׁים` → *he had* … *wives* puts *had* on `הָיָה` and *he* on the suffix. **The existential particle `יֵשׁ` is read on exactly those terms.** Where `יֵשׁ` stands in the clause it is what the *have* renders, exactly as a written `הָיָה` is: the particle takes the word and heads on it, its preposition goes `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun — `יֶשׁ־לִי תִקְוָה` → ***I have*** *hope* gives *have* to `יֵשׁ`, *I* to the suffix and nothing to the `לְ`. This is rule 50's reading of the Aramaic positive existential `אִיתַי`, which takes whatever overt finite frame the ASV writes for it, a *have* among them, and of the negative `אַיִן`, which keeps the frame and heads on its own word in all twenty-eight of its corpus units rather than leaving it to a morpheme standing beside it. Read the condition and not the lemma, as rule 40 directs: what makes such a clause possessive is the existential, and a written `יֵשׁ` left `unrepresented` beside a preposition holding the *have* would leave the clause's one predicating morpheme with nothing, against rule 2. Where the clause is verbless and no existential particle stands in it, the possessive preposition is what makes it possessive and carries the *have*: `לָהֶם מִסְגְּרוֹת` → *they had panels* puts *had* on `לְ` and *they* on the suffix, and `שָׁפְרָה עָלָי` → *I have a goodly heritage* puts *have* on `עַל` and *I* on the suffix. Where neither is present, a possessive suffix can be the possession by itself and takes the supplied verb with its pronoun: `טוֹבָתִי בַּל עָלֶיךָ` → *I have no good beyond thee* gives the suffix *I have*, headed on the pronoun. Another finite verb in the clause does not qualify merely by being finite. `שָׁפְרָה` is not a copula: the ASV renders it by the attributive *goodly*, which is its lexeme, so the *have* is not its. **But a verb the ASV has itself rendered by the *have* does qualify, and the same subtraction decides it.** Where the Hebrew writes a verb of falling or allotment and the English writes *have* in its place — `יִפְּלוּ בְנַחֲלָה` → *they shall have inheritance* — dropping the word leaves that verb with no rendering at all, so the *have* is the verb's own together with the subject pronoun rule 17 keeps there, and a preposition beside it whose relation the ASV has left unstated goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **And where nothing in the clause makes it possessive, the word is not to be placed at all.** A clause that writes no `הָיָה`, no existential particle, no possessive preposition, no suffix and no verb the *have* renders has no morpheme to carry it: `יוֹסֵף חֲבָלִים` → *Joseph* ***shall have two*** *portions* leaves the supplied verb its own `added` unit under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause, together with any numeral, subject or object the ASV supplies alongside it, while the possessed noun keeps only its own word. Do not fold such a word into that noun, into a neighbouring clause's verb, or into a preposition standing elsewhere in the verse to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and*: it is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. **But that count runs over the morphemes of a clause the Hebrew wrote, and does not reach a *have* the ASV writes inside its recasting of a single nominal.** Where the Hebrew writes a noun of possession — `בַּעַל`, or another noun naming the owner or master of what follows — and the ASV recasts that noun together with its construct dependents as an English head noun and a relative clause of having, rule 46's closing paragraph governs: the supplied antecedent, the relative and the *have* all belong to that noun's own unit, because the *have* is what the noun's own lexeme names, and the unit heads on the *have* under rule 31, while the dependent keeps only its own English. `בַּעַל כְּנָפַיִם` → *that which* ***hath*** *wings* is one unit on `בַּעַל`, headed on *hath*, with *wings* left to `כָּנָף`. So ask whether what the ASV recast is a clause or a nominal before counting a *have* as unlicensed, and do not mark such a word `added` on the ground that the morpheme carrying it is not a verb. Test by subtraction, as in rule 16 — drop the *have* and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If only the possession relation is gone, the *have* is the preposition's or the suffix's; if a written verb, a written existential particle, or a written noun of possession is left with nothing, it is that morpheme's; and if nothing in the clause is diminished but a possession the English has supplied, it is `added`. **Read *no possessive preposition* and *no suffix* in that count as none the ASV has left an English word for.** A preposition or a suffix on which the ASV has already spent its own word stands in the same position as an absent one: it is not what makes the clause possessive, and it is not a home for a second English word, exactly as rule 52 counts a preposition's function words against the morphemes that could carry them and rule 51 says a waw holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one. What this rule's earlier sentences govern is a `בְּ` or a `לְ` that is itself the clause's predicate, for which the ASV writes no preposition at all — `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* — and not a locative or other phrase the ASV has rendered in full. `אוֹ תְבַלֻּל בְּעֵינוֹ` → *or* ***that hath*** *a blemish in his eye* writes *in* for the `בְּ`, *his* for the suffix, *eye* for the noun and *a blemish* for `תְּבַלֻּל`, so nothing is left for the *hath* to complete and it is its own `added` unit; `מְרוֹחַ אָשֶׁךְ` → ***hath his*** *stones broken* goes the same way, the adjective keeping *broken* and the noun *stones*, with the supplied *his* `added` besides under rule 18's closing sentence. Count the clause's English words against the morphemes that could carry them before reaching for one that is already spent. **And where the possessive clause is a relative clause, count the ASV's words against the morphemes that could carry them before placing the English subject.** Where the ASV writes one word for the relative and the resumption together, that word is the relative's and it supplies the subject: `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* gives *that* to `אֲשֶׁר` and *hath* to the `בְּ`, and the suffix is `unrepresented` under rule 22, since two morphemes point at the antecedent and the ASV writes one word for it. **But where the ASV writes a subject pronoun besides the relative, two English words answer to the two morphemes and neither is a surplus.** `כֹּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ` → *all* ***that he hath*** gives *that* to `אֲשֶׁר`, *hath* to the possessive `לְ` and *he* to the suffix, which is the subject pronoun this rule's earlier sentences give it; the same clause written without a relative gives the suffix that pronoun in any case, as `מוּם בּוֹ` → *he hath a blemish* does. Count as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` beside a written pronoun no other morpheme answers to, which would leave that pronoun `added` against rule 30 while the morpheme it realizes held nothing. A written `הָיָה` in such a clause still takes the *have* itself and leaves both the preposition and the suffix `unrepresented`: `אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish*. **And an interrogative particle standing in such a clause does not take the *have* either.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a disjunctive question, stands in a possessive clause and the ASV marks the question by fronting the possessive verb itself, that word is the possessive morpheme's under this rule's earlier sentences and the particle is `unrepresented` under rule 17's sentence on a question marked by inversion alone: `וְאִם־זְרוֹעַ כָּאֵל לָךְ` → *Or* ***hast*** *thou an arm like God* gives *hast* to the `לְ` and *thou* to its suffix, and leaves the `אִם` nothing. Rule 20's fronted-copula sentence and rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause reach a copula the construction supplies and an existential frame, which are words no other morpheme licenses; a *have* is neither, since this rule assigns it to the `הָיָה`, the existential particle, the preposition, the suffix, the verb or the noun of possession that makes the clause possessive, and handing it to the particle would leave that morpheme holding nothing while the relation it alone carries went unrendered, against rule 2. Read what the fronted word is rather than that the clause is a question: where the ASV writes a separate question auxiliary besides the *have* — a *Do*, a *Shall* or a *Will* at the clause head — that word is the particle's under rule 17 as before, and the *have* still goes where this rule sends it.
amendments.why: RUT.1.12 (`כִּי אָמַרְתִּי יֶשׁ־לִי תִקְוָה` → *If I should say, I have hope*) met a case rule 43 had not considered: the Hebrew positive existential `יֵשׁ`. The rule's enumeration names `הָיָה`, the possessive preposition, a bare suffix, a verb rendered by the *have*, and a noun of possession, and its *Where the clause is verbless* sentence — read literally, since `יֵשׁ` is a particle and not a verb — would have handed the *have* to `לִי`, left the clause's one predicating morpheme `unrepresented`, and put the suffix's pronoun nowhere. The chapter aligned it the other way on the analogy of rule 50, which already gives the Aramaic positive existential `אִיתַי` whatever overt finite frame the ASV writes for it, *have* included, and which heads existential `אַיִן` on its own word in all 28 corpus units rather than on the frame English supplies. Amended rather than promoted a new rule, because the sentence that misleads is inside rule 43 and a cross-reference would have left it standing for whoever read it first; the change is the added `יֵשׁ` sentence, the *and no existential particle stands in it* qualification on the verbless sentence, and `existential particle` added to the two enumerations that count what can carry the word. No rule text was removed.

conventions: English kinship compounds render one Hebrew noun and are one unit: כַּלָּה → daughter in law, daughters in law (vv. 6, 7, 8, 22), חֲמוֹת → mother in law (v. 14), יְבֶמֶת → sister in law (v. 15, twice). The words in law stand inside that noun's unit — never split off, never added, never given to a neighbouring morpheme — and the head is the first word under rule 31's subtraction, since in law names nothing on its own. A suffix on the noun takes its own possessive under rule 18 and stands outside the compound.

An English particle written with שׁוּב belongs to that verb: turn again (vv. 11, 12), is gone back (v. 15), hath brought me home again (v. 21). None of the bare verbs the ASV chooses for it — turn, go, bring — writes the returning, so rule 44's first condition is unmet and the particle is never surplus. Contrast הָלַךְ in v. 21, where went already writes the going and the supplied out states a direction no morpheme in the clause writes, so that word is its own added unit. This is the line the chapter draws between rule 44's kept particle and its surplus one; yatsa keeps its forth in vv. 7 and 13 on the first ground.

The distributive אִשָּׁה of vv. 8 and 9 is rendered by the whole partitive phrase each of you, which is that noun's own rendering, headed on each. The of belongs to no other morpheme and neither word is added; rule 15's partitive-quantifier sentence does not reach it, because a morpheme standing in the clause licenses the expression.

Count as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` beside a written pronoun no other morpheme answers to, which would leave that pronoun `added` against rule 30 while the morpheme it realizes held nothing. A written `הָיָה` in such a clause still takes the *have* itself and leaves both the preposition and the suffix `unrepresented`: `אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish*. **And an interrogative particle standing in such a clause does not take the *have* either.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a disjunctive question, stands in a possessive clause and the ASV marks the question by fronting the possessive verb itself, that word is the possessive morpheme's under this rule's earlier sentences and the particle is `unrepresented` under rule 17's sentence on a question marked by inversion alone: `וְאִם־זְרוֹעַ כָּאֵל לָךְ` → *Or* ***hast*** *thou an arm like God* gives *hast* to the `לְ` and *thou* to its suffix, and leaves the `אִם` nothing. Rule 20's fronted-copula sentence and rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause reach a copula the construction supplies and an existential frame, which are words no other morpheme licenses; a *have* is neither, since this rule assigns it to the `הָיָה`, the existential particle, the preposition, the suffix, the verb or the noun of possession that makes the clause possessive, and handing it to the particle would leave that morpheme holding nothing while the relation it alone carries went unrendered, against rule 2. Read what the fronted word is rather than that the clause is a question: where the ASV writes a separate question auxiliary besides the *have* — a *Do*, a *Shall* or a *Will* at the clause head — that word is the particle's under rule 17 as before, and the *have* still goes where this rule sends it.
amended.why: RUT.1.12 (`כִּי אָמַרְתִּי יֶשׁ־לִי תִקְוָה` → *If I should say, I have hope*) met a case rule 43 had not considered: the Hebrew positive existential `יֵשׁ`. The rule's enumeration names `הָיָה`, the possessive preposition, a bare suffix, a verb rendered by the *have*, and a noun of possession, and its *Where the clause is verbless* sentence — read literally, since `יֵשׁ` is a particle and not a verb — would have handed the *have* to `לִי`, left the clause's one predicating morpheme `unrepresented`, and put the suffix's pronoun nowhere. The chapter aligned it the other way on the analogy of rule 50, which already gives the Aramaic positive existential `אִיתַי` whatever overt finite frame the ASV writes for it, *have* included, and which heads existential `אַיִן` on its own word in all 28 corpus units rather than on the frame English supplies. Amended rather than promoted a new rule, because the sentence that misleads is inside rule 43 and a cross-reference would have left it standing for whoever read it first; the change is the added `יֵשׁ` sentence, the *and no existential particle stands in it* qualification on the verbless sentence, and `existential particle` added to the two enumerations that count what can carry the word. No rule text was removed.

report: Checked all 46 candidate lemma groups and, separately, the six `added` units the lemma table is blind to (v.12 *your way*, v.12 *if*, v.16 *and*, v.17 *aught but*, v.19 *the women*, v.21 *out*). No construction is analysed two ways with nothing in the source licensing the difference, so patches is empty.

Near-misses resolved rather than patched. הֲ has three treatments — v.13 fronted *would* (rule 17), v.19 fronted *Is* (rule 20), v.11 `unrepresented` because rule 43 keeps the *have* on the possessive לְ — each fixed by what the ASV wrote and by what else stands in the clause. לְ before an infinitive divides by whether the ASV writes a function word at all (rule 52): *to*, *in*, *when* in vv. 1, 6, 7, 16, 18 against the bare gerund *speaking* in v.18.

The אֲשֶׁר fusions head on the relative (v.7 *where*, v.16 *whither* and *where*, v.17 *where*) while כַּאֲשֶׁר → *as* (v.8) and עַד אֲשֶׁר → *till* (v.13) head on the governing first morpheme. That is rule 22 against rule 23, both named there, and not a split.

Construct chains are counted consistently: שֵׁם with an article-bearing rectum in vv. 2 and 4 takes rule 29's arthrous reading in both (supplied *the* on the construct, written *the* on the article, *of* on the rectum), and the multi-level chains of v.2 (*of his two sons*) and v.22 (*of barley harvest*) both put the *of* on the immediate rectum with the competing reading named in the note. שְׁנֵי plus suffix follows the ASV: *both of them* splits under rule 19's suffix-rectum sentence in v.5, *they two* leaves the suffix a bare *they* in v.19.

BSB: no genuine error. The 19 R disagreements are the documented rule 40 convention — datives and objects the ASV promotes to bare English objects in vv. 4, 6, 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 20, 21 — plus rule 21's resultative לְ. v.5 גַם is unrendered because *both of them* is fully accounted for by שְׁנֵי and its suffix under rule 19; v.7 Sd is silenced by the *where* fusion, which carries no motion; v.11 Ti is rule 43's own ruling that the fronted *have* is the possessive preposition's and the question is marked by inversion; v.12 and v.17 Td are articles the ASV writes no *the* for (*to night*, *death*); v.18's waw opens an apodosis the ASV writes bare.

Three single-verse ties were left standing with their competing readings already named under rule 8, rather than reopened here: v.1 *a certain man* read as one indefinite nominal expression (competitor: *certain* `added`), v.17 *more* on יָסַף against *also* on the second כֹּה (competitor: the reverse), v.12 מִן → *too … to* headed on *too* as rule 24's phrase turning on a content word (competitor: *to*). The v.13 correction of לְבִלְתִּי → *from* into one fused unit headed on the negative was carried in the verse file and stands.

One contract gap the chapter met and had to settle by analogy: the Hebrew positive existential יֵשׁ in a possessive clause (v.12, *I have hope*). Rule 43's enumeration names הָיָה, the possessive preposition, a bare suffix, a verb and a noun of possession, and its *where the clause is verbless* sentence would on a literal reading have handed the *have* to לִי and left יֵשׁ holding nothing. Amended rule 43 rather than adding a rule, so the over-broad sentence is corrected where it stands.
